Consult Summary:
- Telemedicine consult for a 26-year-old male with known asthma presenting with 3 hours of chest tightness, mild exertional dyspnea, wheeze, and nonproductive cough after a recent viral URI; assessed as an acute asthma exacerbation and provided inhaler refills, spacer, and a 5-day oral steroid course with safety-net advice.

History:
- Presenting complaint: Chest tightness for ~3 hours.
- Symptom details:
  - Dyspnea: Mild; worse with exertion (walking up stairs); not short of breath at rest.
  - Wheeze present.
  - Cough: Nonproductive; persists since recent cold; slightly worse at night but generally consistent.
  - Denies chest pain; describes tightness rather than pain.
- Recent illness: Viral URI last week (sore throat, runny nose, feeling unwell). URI symptoms improving except cough.
- Asthma context:
  - Ran out of inhalers about a week ago and has not used preventer or reliever since then.
  - Concerned due to prior severe exacerbation requiring intubation in high school; has not had a severe episode in a long time.
- Exacerbating factors: Physical exertion (stairs); recent viral illness; lack of inhaler use.
- Relieving factors: None reported (no inhalers available).
- Associated symptoms: No sputum production.
- Pertinent negatives: Not short of breath at rest; no chest pain.

Past Medical History:
- Asthma
  - Background: Longstanding; prior severe exacerbation requiring hospital admission and intubation at ~age 16–17.
  - Current status: Off inhalers for ~1 week due to running out; now symptomatic.
  - Associated medications:
    - Salbutamol (Ventolin) inhaler – dose/route/frequency not documented (currently out).
    - Beclometasone (Clenil Modulite) inhaler – dose/route/frequency not documented (currently out).
- Allergic rhinitis/hay fever and dust allergy.
- Childhood eczema.
- Childhood milk protein allergy.
- Allergies: No known drug allergies.

Social History:
- Recently away at university last week.
- Work: Doctor discussed rest and self-certification for up to 7 days; specific occupation not documented.
- Tobacco, alcohol, substance use: Not documented.

Family History:
- Mother: Eczema.
- Father: Asthma.

Physical Examination:
- Vitals: Not documented.
- Exam findings: Not documented.
- Functional status reported: Not short of breath at rest; increased shortness of breath with stairs. No peak flow available.

Investigations:
- None performed or documented.

Assessment & Plan:
- Issue 1: Acute asthma exacerbation likely triggered by recent viral URI and lapse in controller/reliever inhalers.
  - Prescriptions to be sent within the hour:
    - Salbutamol (Ventolin) inhaler – PRN use; specific dose not documented.
    - Beclometasone (Clenil Modulite) inhaler – resume maintenance; advised morning use once improved; dose not documented.
    - Spacer device provided; instructions to use with inhalers to improve delivery.
  - Oral steroid course: Steroid tablets (specific drug/strength not documented) – take 2 tablets in the morning for 5 days.
  - Counseling on steroid side effects: Possible mood changes (low or high), elevated blood sugar, rash, nausea, headache; advised to read medication leaflet; generally well tolerated.
  - Safety-net and escalation:
    - Seek medical attention if needing salbutamol more often than every 3 hours.
    - Urgent care if worsening shortness of breath, chest tightness/pain, light-headedness, or any concerning deterioration.
  - Rest advised; self-certify for up to 7 days if needed.
- Issue 2: Ongoing allergic rhinitis/dust allergy (comorbidity relevant to asthma).
  - No specific treatment changes discussed today.
- General plan items:
  - Reinforce inhaler adherence and technique (spacer use); spacer provided with instructions (prime, then 5–10 breaths per dose).
  - Follow-up: Not specifically scheduled; advised to seek care if symptoms worsen or do not improve.

Quality checks:
- Missing expected elements:
  - No vitals, oxygen saturation, peak flow, or physical exam documented.
  - Exact steroid name and dose not documented.
  - Inhaler doses/frequencies not documented.
  - Full medication reconciliation (other meds/supplements) not documented.
  - Smoking/alcohol/substance history not documented.
  - Specific follow-up appointment/timeframe not documented.
  - Exact date of birth (day) not documented.
- Internal conflicts:
  - Patient name conflict: Doctor initially referenced “Brian,” patient identified as “Daniel” (conflict noted).
- Transcript quality: Generally clear; brief audio dropouts noted when discussing prior steroid use.
